rv.q: This play will make you shiver, for so many reasons.

Over the course of the two-hour, interval-less production, one of the onlookers, Jessica Gunning, takes on an increasingly active role. She takes on the guise of Mrs Jewkes, the complicit housekeeper in Richardson's novel, and, in the production's most potent moment, she sings a song, rather beautif...

Mitchell's production is sexually explicit, but I can only assume that anyone shocked by the play's arguments about the overthrow of oppressive masculinity and the malleability of gender must have spent the last decade in monastic seclusion.
Mitchell’s twitchy, febrile direction and a fine electronic score from Melanie Wilson give it a sense of depth, but I can’t help but think the play itself is kind of shallow.
In Katie Mitchell’s production it is both bludgeoning and baffling.
Cate Blanchett live on stage, wearing black stockings and a strap-on dildo, giving her husband one up the bum... and it's still really tedious. That's how bad this new Martin Crimp play is.
The action itself is slow and stuttering, but the scenario’s riveting — laced with subtext, laden with history and loaded with threat.
The arguments are interesting, and the Woman is definitely empowered.
The show's ending becomes a little earnest and predictable and the twist involving the shrink is weak.
She puts her charisma and commitment entirely in the service of the play.
It takes a special kind of badness to make Cate Blanchett lubing up a strap-on boring, but the National Theatre managed it.
By then, all the hullabaloo surrounding this play has devolved into a sigh of “So what?”: less torture, as it turns out, than torpor.
Whether they’ll still be fans when they’ve sat through this pretentious, self congratulatory drivel is another matter.
For once the hype is justified: this is clearly the best new play on the London stage.
Little is clear for much of the play's uninterrupted 100 minutes or so.
This really is a long, drawn-out and misty affair that has glimpses of clarity but cannot be saved, even by some strong performances.
Crimp's enactment of fluid sexual roles and patriarchal power play is drier than a gender studies lecture.

cn.t: Critics find Martin Crimp's sexually explicit play a disappointing waste of talent despite Cate Blanchett's star power. Most deem it tedious, baffling, and underpropelled, though some praise its exploration of power dynamics.
